content.overview: BNS s. 39 — When such right extends to causing any harm other than death.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
When such right extends to causing any harm other than death. BNS restatement of IPC 101. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 101. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 39 is the rule on “When such right extends to causing any harm other than death”. The section provides that if the offence be not of any of the descriptions specified in section 38, the right of private defence of the body does not extend to the voluntary causing of death to the assailant, but does extend, under the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing to the assailant of any harm other than death. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 39 exists so that “When such right extends to causing any harm other than death” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
39. If the offence be not of any of the descriptions specified in section 38, the right of private defence of the body does not extend to the voluntary causing of death to the assailant, but does extend, under the restrictions specified in section 37, to the voluntary causing to the assailant of any harm other than death

learningObjectives: Understand the scope of non-lethal private defence of the body under BNS s. 39.
Identify the boundary: applies to bodily offences NOT enumerated in s. 38.
Apply the negative restriction: does NOT extend to causing death.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 39 provides that if the offence be not of any of the descriptions enumerated in section 38, the right of private defence of the body does not extend to the voluntary causing of death to the assailant, but does extend, under the restrictions mentioned in section 37, to the voluntary causing to the assailant of any harm other than death.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: When an unlawful bodily assault does not threaten death, grievous hurt, rape, or other supreme bodily hazards, the victim cannot kill the assailant, but is entitled to inflict any necessary non-lethal harm (blows, cuts, fractures) to ward off the attack.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 39 (corresponding to IPC s. 101).
Negative boundary: Offence does NOT fall under s. 38 descriptions.
Harm limit: Prohibits 'voluntary causing of death'.
Permitted harm: Extends to causing 'any harm other than death', subject to s. 37 proportionality.
essentialIngredients: An offence affecting the human body is committed or attempted.
The offence is NOT of any description listed in s. 38.
The defender does not voluntarily cause death.
The defender inflicts non-lethal harm within s. 37 necessity.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 39 covers the wide array of ordinary bodily assaults: slaps, simple hurt, pushing, minor threats, or scuffles. If an attacker approaches with bare fists threatening a black eye, the defender has every right to strike him with fists, push him to the ground, or use a stick to repel him. However, the defender CANNOT pull out a pistol and shoot the attacker dead. Doing so violates s. 39 and s. 37(4), forfeiting complete private defence and reducing the offence to culpable homicide under Exception 2 of murder.
examples: Teaching example (Repelling simple hurt): A person is attacked by an aggressive rival who tries to slap and kick him. The victim punches the attacker in the jaw, knocking him down and dislocating his tooth. Section 39 protects the victim; non-lethal harm was justified.

Teaching example (Lethal reaction to simple slap): An assailant slaps a person across the cheek. The person draws a revolver and shoots the assailant through the heart. Section 39 bars causing death for simple assault; the person is guilty of culpable homicide.
distinctions: Section 38 vs Section 39: Section 38 authorizes causing death for 7 grave perils; Section 39 strictly prohibits causing death for all other bodily offences.
Justified non-lethal harm vs Exceeding private defence: Non-lethal harm is fully justified; exceeding the limit by causing death results in culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
problemApplication: Issue: What is the criminal liability of an accused who broke the leg of an unarmed assailant who was attempting to push him into a ditch?
Rule: BNS s. 39 permits voluntary causing of any harm other than death for assaults not covered by s. 38, subject to s. 37.

Application: Pushing into a ditch threatens simple or moderate hurt, not death or grievous hurt. Fracturing the leg was reasonably necessary to prevent being thrown into the ditch, and death was not caused.
Conclusion: Section 39 applies; the accused is protected.

shortAnswer: State BNS s. 39 rule: non-lethal defence for non-s.38 offences.
Emphasize: death must NOT be voluntarily caused.
tenMark: Introduction: The boundary between lethal and non-lethal private defence.
Application to simple hurt, assault, and minor scuffles.
Consequence of exceeding the right: reduction from murder to culpable homicide.
sixteenMark: Introduction: Proportionality in defence of body.
Textual analysis of BNS s. 39 in conjunction with s. 38.
The distinction between simple assault and grave bodily hazards.
The legal effect of exceeding the right: Exception 2 to murder (culpable homicide).
Judicial application in rural affrays and sudden quarrels.

keyTakeaways: Applies to all bodily assaults not enumerated in s. 38.
Strictly bars the voluntary causing of death.
Permits any non-lethal harm proportionate to the threat.
